Subgroup analysis based on baseline HBeAg status was not considered informative, as the majority of studies (77% in Q1 and 100% in Q2) were conducted on populations with more than 90% HBeAg-positive individuals. 3. When analyzed by drug class, very few studies utilized nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) compared to interferon (IFN) and pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN). 4. A trend was observed suggesting higher efficacy of IFN/PEG-IFN compared to NAs for HBV DNA suppression, HBeAg loss, and HBeAg seroconversion. However, NAs demonstrated higher efficacy than IFN/PEG-IFN for ALT normalization. These differences in efficacy between subgroups were not statistically significant. 5. Among the included studies, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) accounted for 35% in Q1 and 89% in Q2. Prospective studies made up 47% in Q1 and 16% in Q2, while retrospective studies accounted for 16% in Q1 and 16% in Q2. 6. Most studies were published before 2014 (70% in Q1 and 67% in Q2), with fewer studies published since 2014 (28% in Q1 and 33% in Q2). 7. The majority of studies were conducted in the Western Pacific Region (33% in Q1 and 22% in Q2) and the European Region (35% in Q1 and 39% in Q2). Other regions, such as South-East Asia, Eastern Mediterranean, African, and the Americas, had minimal representation. 8. Interferon-based regimens were the most commonly studied antiviral therapies, with IFN used in 61% of Q2 studies and PEG-IFN in 16%. Nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) were used in 22% of Q2 studies, with specific drugs like adefovir, entecavir, lamivudine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate each accounting for 16%. Combination therapy was reported in 11% of Q2 studies. 9. The quality of evidence for treatment efficacy in children and adolescents was rated as low, with outcomes reported as risk ratios (RR) or hazard ratios (HR) pooled from RCTs and non-RCTs. 10. Point-of-care (POC) HBV DNA viral load (VL) testing offers an alternative to centralized laboratory-based standard-of-care VL assays, aiming to accelerate diagnosis and treatment. 11. POC HBV DNA testing demonstrated a turnaround time of less than one day for VL results in some studies, compared to 7–11 days in others. 12. The time from receiving DNA testing results to treatment initiation ranged from 1 to 8 days in studies reporting this outcome. 13. Overall turnaround time from a positive HBsAg test to treatment initiation was less than one day in one study and 27 days in another. 14. Comparative data for non-POC testing was limited, with one study reporting a turnaround time of 2 weeks to 2 months for DNA VL test results and 26 days from receiving results to treatment initiation. 15. HBV POC DNA testing appears to be associated with high rates of DNA testing and treatment initiation among eligible individuals, with a turnaround time of less than one day for VL results. 16. More studies are needed to establish the effects of POC HBV DNA testing compared to non-POC testing on the HBV care cascade. 17. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a significant global public health issue, with only 10% of those infected diagnosed and 2% receiving treatment. 18. HBV DNA quantification is critical for determining treatment eligibility, antiviral prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child transmission, and treatment monitoring. 19. WHO and other professional guidelines recommend using sensitive nucleic acid amplification tests for HBV DNA quantification. 20. Limited access to laboratory-based HBV DNA assays in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, poses a significant barrier to widespread uptake and initiation of hepatitis B treatment. 21. High-quality evidence supports the clinical impact of POC assays for HIV viral load monitoring, early infant diagnosis, tuberculosis diagnosis, and HCV VL testing. 22. POC HCV VL assays have demonstrated reduced turnaround times and increased RNA testing and treatment uptake compared to laboratory-based RNA testing. 23. There is limited data and no prior systematic review on the use of POC HBV DNA assays to improve access to HBV DNA quantification for determining treatment eligibility and uptake. 24. The increasing availability of POC platforms for use in HIV and TB care, as well as during the COVID-19 pandemic, presents an opportunity to expand their application to HBV care. 25. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate the impact of POC HBV VL assays compared to laboratory-based standard-of-care assays on HBV DNA testing, treatment uptake, and turnaround times. 26. The study followed Cochrane guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023398440). 27. Seven studies (10 arms, 9462 participants) were included, with most conducted in lowor middle-income countries. 28. Six studies used POC assays on-site, two used mobile units, and four were laboratory-based. 29. The most common model of care involved testing and treatment at the same site but during different visits. 30. High heterogeneity was observed across studies within each model-of-care category for all outcomes. 31. The quality of evidence was rated as low, highlighting the need for further research.
